title: TCS CEO Says Traditional IT Growth Will Taper as AI Revenue Crosses $3 Billion
excerpt: K. Krithivasan's BusinessLine interview puts a number on the pivot — $3 billion in annualized AI revenue, up 19% in a quarter — as the old services model slows.
body:
• TCS chief executive K. Krithivasan told The Hindu BusinessLine that growth in traditional IT services will taper as enterprises redirect spending toward AI and newer technology services.
  • The company disclosed that annualized AI revenue has crossed $3 billion — more than a tenth of the business — up from $2.6 billion in the June quarter to $3.1 billion by end-September, a 19% jump in one quarter.
  • COO Aarthi Subramanian framed AI as an "efficiency multiplier rather than a cannibalizing force" — automation frees capacity that gets redirected to new client projects.
  • What this means for you: for the lakhs of Indian tech workers in the US on H-1Bs and green-card queues — TCS is one of eight firms just suspended from the PERM programme — the message is clear: AI skills are becoming the price of admission, not a bonus.

The head of India's largest IT services company has put a number on the industry's AI pivot — and a warning on its old business model. In an interview with The Hindu BusinessLine, published October 12, Tata Consultancy Services chief executive K. Krithivasan said growth in traditional IT services will taper as clients shift spending toward AI and newer technology services, with the decline offset "in a significant way" by AI-led business.

The $3 billion disclosure

The headline figure: TCS's annualized AI revenue has crossed $3 billion — over a tenth of the company — rising from $2.6 billion in the June quarter to $3.1 billion by the end of September, a 19% increase in a single quarter. TCS is one of the few large Indian IT firms to disclose an annualized AI number at all, and the disclosure is a deliberate signal: in a market that has punished Indian IT stocks on fears of AI disruption, TCS wants the AI business measured, not rumored.

https://x.com/WealthEnrich/status/2109478827982467515

Krithivasan said customers are only "scratching the surface" of AI opportunities — spanning AI model and asset strategy, agent architecture, data and technology modernization, and AI-led business outcomes. Over the past six months, he said, clients have talked less about macroeconomic uncertainty and more about AI opportunities, which enterprises now see as something "they cannot afford to defer."

"AI is an efficiency multiplier rather than a cannibalizing force."

— Aarthi Subramanian, Chief Operating Officer, TCS

Efficiency multiplier — or margin threat?

The optimistic framing comes from COO Aarthi Subramanian: automation-driven productivity frees capacity that can be redirected to new customer projects, so transformation demand outpaces internal efficiency gains. But the interview also acknowledged the headwind the market is actually pricing in: clients are demanding that AI productivity gains show up in their bills, pushing contracts toward fixed-cost and outcome-based models rather than paying for manpower. That is the mechanism behind the margin anxiety — AI as a growth driver, in BusinessLine's companion piece — and it is structural, not cyclical.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=nPjJqpA0cN0

The tension showed up in the September quarter itself: TCS delivered its weakest sequential revenue growth in three years even as AI revenue surged, and discretionary IT spending remains under scrutiny. Days earlier, Reuters reported that senior staff at C3A grade and above missed quarterly variable pay after the company missed internal targets — the first time in at least two years, according to an internal memo from CHRO Sudeep Kunnumal. The stock, notably, rose as much as 6.2% on the AI-revenue uptick.

What it means for Indian tech talent

For the diaspora, the interview lands in a charged week. TCS is among the eight firms the US Labor Department suspended from the PERM green-card programme on October 8, and the company's AI pivot is the other half of the same story: the Indian IT employment model — large benches of engineers deployed on long-term maintenance contracts — is being rewritten from both ends, by immigration restrictions in the US and automation everywhere.

Krithivasan's thesis, stripped of corporate framing, is that the tapering is inevitable and the only question is whether AI revenue grows fast enough to replace what traditional services lose. At $3 billion annualized and 19% quarterly growth, TCS has bought itself the right to make that argument. The next earnings call will show whether investors buy it too.
